refutation.item: rivals/r5-m03-rival.turn2 p5 (and p4); held-out t64 from result-6f1bb7
refutation.note: The theory says the plain-register answers are 'wrong about half the time whatever the problem's difficulty'. In the turn-2 duel tests the plain base's non-self-opening answers are far more accurate on cued-4/4 problems than on cued <=1/4 problems: +0.23 at T 1.0 (n 304) and +0.49 at T 0.6 (n 226). Both intervals exclude 0, and 'theory_should_say' put both near 0. This is the theory's own register on its own prompt, so the scope does not exclude it. The defend agent shaded its predictions to 0.41 and 0.63 and still lost both tests (gains -0.63 and -1.11). Held out: on the board result result-6f1bb7 (base - 8 directions, cue, hard328), 118/328 right, against the advocate's claim 150 [139, 161], gain -3.0. This edit is size -1 with the cue, so it is only loosely in scope. I also read result-07f566 (the 22 quick finished-wrong answers, recomputed by abaybektursun), result-ad3c24 and result-d2933e (top8 plain 427/500, 88/100). None of these contradict the mixture picture.

wins_judgement: The offline gains (p1 +2.77, p2 +3.0, p3 +3.0) come from facts that were already on the board. Round 05 computed the 22 quick wrong answers, which sit on cued-easy problems and are short (result-07f566). This theory is the round-05 rival built to fit those numbers, and its own rival 'why_strongest' notes that it reproduces all three values. So a reader with that board item would have reached them. Only the mixture mechanism makes them hang together, but the three tests do not separate it from a prompt-keyed account. In the duel, the one gain the mechanism really earned is p2 (+3.0, n 401, separating): the plain base's T 1.0 wrong rate on top8's quick-wrong problems is no higher than on top8-right, cued-easy problems (-0.057 [-0.23, 0.13]). That supports per-sample rather than per-problem failure. p1, p3 and p6 also lean toward the theory, but they are flagged same_prediction and add 0. Held out: t65 and t66 are inside the claimed intervals but give nothing over the readers (-0.18 and about 0). t64 is a large miss (-3.0).
rival: The rival is a prompt-keyed plain-base failure: top8's quick wrong answers fall on the problems that the plain base itself gets wrong. It explains p1-p3 just as well. The only separating test is duel p2, which favours the theory (+3.0; measured -0.057 against the rival's 0.25 [0.06, 0.44]). I read p2.py: it implements the recipe as written. Group Q is top8 score_v3 0, not a cap hit, at most 2,000 tokens, first row per problem. Group C is top8-right problems with exactly 4 attempt-0 cued rows and at least 3 of them right. T3 is regraded with v3, and wrong means v3 = 0 or a cap hit. It uses a bootstrap interval, plus an alt variant that gives -0.055. The rival wins on difficulty dependence (p4, p5), where the theory's 'whatever the difficulty' clause fails. Here both are flagged same_prediction because the defend agent hedged. Duel state: not separated from rival (1 separating test, total gain 3.0).

novelty.nearest: Cai et al., 'On Predictability of RL Dynamics for LLMs' (AlphaRL): the Rank-1 subspace of the RL parameter update recovers >99% of RL's reasoning gains when added to the base
novelty.difference: The paper reports aggregate accuracy recovery from a low-rank slice of the RL delta. It does not say that the partial edit acts as a per-sample mixture of RL-like answers and unchanged plain-base answers, or where the residual errors fall.

import_carries_gain.which: The theory imports no published finding. Its winning claims rest on the board's own row files (WSP-1 top8 plain, Day-1 #3 cued base, T3), not on the low-rank-RL literature.

verdict: weak: the duel state is 'not separated from rival'. The theory wins only one separating duel test (p2, n 401; stands needs two), and its own clause that plain-register errors ignore difficulty is contradicted by duel tests p4/p5 (gaps 0.23 and 0.49, intervals excluding 0).
